abstract:
Objective. Determine how many forearm surface electromyography electrodes can be removed while preserving mean gesture recognition for unseen participants, and assess the additional value of attribution-based selection.
Approach. We analyzed 43\ GRABMyo participants using sixteen monopolar electrodes and sixteen active gestures. Participant-disjoint inner cross-fitting estimated TreeSHAP rankings within each outer leave-one-subject-out fold. Reduced models were retrained and compared with full16 using participant-bootstrap intervals and a predefined 0.02 Macro-F1 engineering tolerance. Exploratory checks included primary-budget geometric selection, paired gesture predictions, shared-resource permutation selection, and task, window and classifier sensitivities.
Main results. SHAP12 achieved mean Macro-F1 0.528\ versus 0.541\ for full16; its change was -0.0133\ (95\% CI -0.0160\ to -0.0106). The smallest qualifying count was 12. Nevertheless, 11\ participants lost more than 0.02 and 4\ gestures showed corrected declines. Geometric12 did not establish non-inferiority, and the direct SHAP12 mean advantage remained uncertain (+0.0060; 95\% CI -0.0010\ to +0.0127). Attribution outperformed mean random subsets in the lighter comparison. Shared-resource SHAP outperformed grouped permutation at six electrodes, but its twelve-electrode advantage remained uncertain. Stability regularization did not establish an improvement.
Significance. One quarter of this monopolar array could be removed within the mean tolerance under offline participant-independent evaluation. This validates a selection procedure rather than one locked physical layout; individual losses and uncertain transfer require independent validation before device claims.
